citation: Aughey RJ, Hammond K, Varley MC, Schmidt WF, Bourdon PC, Buchheit M et al. 2013, Br J Sports Med (ISA3600)
population: 20 Australian U17 (sea-level natives) and 19 Bolivian U20 (altitude natives) elite youth soccer players
design: Prospective field study, GPS match activity profile
effect: Total distance per minute reduced by a small magnitude in the first match at altitude in BOTH teams; peak 5-min distance reduced in every altitude match vs near sea level; reduction larger (small ES) in Australians than Bolivians in game 4; no clear team difference in maximal accelerations.
limitations: Youth players; only 5 matches; effect-size language ('small', 'moderate') rather than % values in abstract; Bolivians had just descended then re-ascended.
relevance: Stamina / high-intensity running. Key: neither 13 days of acclimatisation nor lifelong residence fully protected match running.

citation: Buchheit M, Simpson BM, Garvican-Lewis LA, Hammond K, Kley M, Schmidt WF et al. 2013, Br J Sports Med (ISA3600)
population: Same ISA3600 cohorts (Australian U17 vs Bolivian U20)
exposure: 2-week camp; Yo-Yo IR1 and 20 m sprint near sea level and on days 3 and 10
design: Prospective field study; wellness questionnaires, HR, HRV, Yo-Yo IR1, 20 m sprint
effect: Australians: moderate-to-large impairment in wellness and Yo-Yo IR1 on arrival relative to Bolivians; acclimatisation substantially slower in Australians; only Bolivians regained near sea-level high-intensity running by camp end. BOTH teams had moderately impaired 20 m sprint at end of camp.
limitations: Youth; no % values in abstract; 20 m sprint decline may reflect fatigue/detraining rather than altitude per se.
relevance: Acclimatisation time course: 2 weeks insufficient for sea-level natives at 3600 m; single-sprint speed did NOT improve at altitude in this study.

citation: Garvican LA, Hammond K, Varley MC, Gore CJ, Billaut F, Aughey RJ 2014, Int J Sports Physiol Perform
exposure: Matches on day 4 and day 6 at altitude; submaximal HR test daily for 10 d
design: Prospective field study, GPS; effect sizes with 90% CI
effect: Day 4 at 1600 m (Denver): total distance -9%, low-velocity running -8%, high-velocity running -15% vs sea-level matches (percentages as summarised by Billaut & Aughey 2013, E31; abstract reports ES -0.76 ± 0.37 for total distance and -0.47 ± 0.59 for high-velocity running). Day 6: total distance still reduced (ES -0.42), high-velocity running no clear effect (ES -0.08). Submaximal HR +5.4% on day 1, back to baseline by day 5.
limitations: Youth; single team; effect sizes not % of distance; no unacclimatised day-1 match.
relevance: Even 1600 m reduces match running for ~6 days; HR (a proxy of acute strain) normalises in ~5 days.

citation: Nassis GP 2013, J Strength Cond Res
population: Professional national teams, 2010 FIFA World Cup (South Africa)
exposure: Tournament matches; acclimatisation status not controlled
design: Retrospective analysis of official FIFA match statistics; one-way ANOVA
effect: Total distance covered 3.1% lower in matches at 1200-1400 m and 1401-1753 m vs sea level (p<0.05). Goals per game and goalkeeper errors leading to goals did not differ with altitude.
limitations: Observational; venue, opponent and heat confounded with altitude; team quality not controlled; only crude technical indices.
relevance: Best professional-level match evidence for a small stamina cost at ~1500 m; no detectable technical cost at that altitude.

citation: Bohner JD, Hoffman JR, McCormack WP et al. 2015, J Hum Kinet
population: 6 NCAA Division I female soccer players
design: Retrospective GPS comparison (2 sea-level matches vs 1 altitude match)
effect: High-intensity running reduced at 1839 m (direction reported; magnitude not retrieved from abstract in this session).
limitations: n=6, single match, female collegiate; magnitude not extracted.
relevance: Supports direction of stamina cost at moderate altitude in a different population.

citation: Wachsmuth N, Kley M, Spielvogel H, Aughey RJ, Gore CJ, Bourdon PC et al. 2013, Br J Sports Med (ISA3600)
population: ISA3600 cohorts: 20 Australian, 19 Bolivian youth players
design: Prospective; CO-rebreathing Hb mass, blood gases, Yo-Yo IR1
effect: Baseline Hb mass higher in Bolivians (12.8 ± 0.8 g/kg) than Australians (11.6 ± 0.7 g/kg). Australians: Hb mass +3.0 ± 2.7% after 12 d; blood volume fell ~400 mL in both teams; PaO2, SaO2 and arterial O2 content fell within 2 h of arrival then partly recovered. Yo-Yo IR1 lower on day 3 than day 10 and related to arterial O2 content. Bolivians' [Hb] fell at sea level (16.6 vs 18.2 g/dL) but Hb mass unchanged.
limitations: Youth; 12 days 'insufficient to reach chronic levels of adaptation'.
relevance: Mechanism for acclimatisation (plasma-volume loss then slow Hb-mass gain) and for the residents' advantage (10% higher Hb mass). Argues against 'fly-in, fly-out'.

citation: Roach GD, Schmidt WF, Aughey RJ, Bourdon PC, Soria R, Claros JCJ et al. 2013, Br J Sports Med (ISA3600)
population: 14 Australian U17 (sea-level) and 12 Bolivian U20 (altitude natives)
design: Prospective field study
effect: Australians: shorter, poorer sleep on first night at altitude; quality normal by end of week 1, quantity still not back to normal after 2 weeks. Bolivians: sleep similar or better at altitude than at sea level.
limitations: Youth; actigraphy only; small n.
relevance: Recovery between matches/training is impaired for sea-level natives for at least 1-2 weeks; residents unaffected.

citation: Sargent C, Schmidt WF, Aughey RJ, Bourdon PC, Soria R, Claros JCJ et al. 2013, Br J Sports Med (ISA3600)
design: Prospective, effect-size statistics
effect: REM sleep lower on arrival, similar to baseline after 2 weeks. Hypopnoeas/desaturations higher on all altitude nights; 50% of players had impaired breathing during sleep that did not improve.
limitations: n=10, youth, no control group.
relevance: Large individual variability: half the squad had disordered breathing in sleep.

citation: McLean BD, Buttifant D, Gore CJ, White K, Kemp J 2013, Br J Sports Med
exposure: 18-19 days, two camps one year apart
design: Repeated-measures; CO-rebreathing Hb mass
effect: Hb mass +3.6 ± 1.6% (camp 1) and +4.4 ± 1.3% (camp 2); individual responsiveness ~half the group mean; same players did not respond consistently year to year (r=0.21).
limitations: Australian Football, not soccer; training camp not competition.
relevance: Individual variability is large and not a fixed trait; do not assume equal acclimatisation across a squad.

citation: McSharry PE 2007, BMJ
altitude: Venue altitude difference up to 3695 m
design: Statistical analysis of match results (win probability, goals for/against vs altitude difference)
effect: Each 1000 m of altitude difference increased goal difference by ~0.5 goal in favour of the higher team. Probability of home win 0.537 for equal-altitude teams vs 0.825 for a 3695 m difference (e.g., Bolivia v Brazil).
limitations: Match results cannot separate altitude physiology from home advantage, travel, crowd, team quality or tactics. Chumacero 2009 (E11) found no significant effect after controlling for team quality.
relevance: Headline 'altitude advantage' estimate; treat as upper bound of combined home + altitude effects.

citation: Chumacero RA 2009, J Sports Econ ('Altitude or Hot Air?')
population: 72 South American World Cup qualifiers (1998, 2002, 2006 cycles)
design: Bivariate Poisson / ordered probit with team-quality controls (FIFA ranking, form)
effect: No statistically significant altitude effect on match outcome or score once team quality is controlled.
limitations: Small sample (72 matches); controls capture long-run quality only.
relevance: Contested evidence: the outcome-level altitude effect is smaller/noisier than McSharry implies.

citation: Cabrera Hernández M, García-Corzo S, Povea Combariza C et al. 2021, J Hum Sport Exerc
altitude: Venues at various altitudes; ascending vs descending
design: Retrospective multinomial regression on results and goals
effect: Home team win probability >50%; authors report that descending (altitude club visiting low altitude) had a greater negative impact on results than ascending.
limitations: Observational club data; confounded by team quality and travel; magnitude not extracted in this session.
relevance: Cautions against assuming altitude clubs gain at sea level.

citation: Tovar J 2014, J Quant Anal Sports ('Gasping for air')
design: Player-level regression with opponent fixed effects
effect: Percentage of successful passes ROSE by ~5.6 percentage points at >2500 m, driven by passing in own half; most other indicators showed no altitude effect. Interpreted as increased risk aversion (behavioural), not improved skill.
limitations: Observational; pass success confounds skill with pass choice; no physiological measures.
relevance: No evidence of a technical-execution decline; players change decisions (safer passes).

citation: Bärtsch P, Saltin B, Dvorak J 2008, Scand J Med Sci Sports (FIFA consensus)
population: FIFA Medical Assessment and Research Centre expert consensus
altitude: Zones: low ~500-2000 m, moderate ~2000-3000 m, high >3000 m
exposure: Recommended acclimatisation: ~3-5 days for low altitude, 1-2 weeks for moderate, >=2 weeks for high altitude
design: Expert consensus
effect: Defines zones: near sea level 0-500 m; low 500-2000 m (minor, detectable aerobic impairment); moderate 2000-3000 m (AMS begins, acclimatisation increasingly important); high 3000-5500 m (performance considerably impaired, AMS clinically relevant). Suggests acclimatisation of 3-5 days for low, 1-2 weeks for moderate, >=2 weeks for high altitude; impact differs for players living at >=1500 m.
limitations: Zone definitions and day-counts summarised from papers citing the consensus (full text not read in this session); consensus, not trial evidence.
relevance: Anchors the 'days since arrival' control.

citation: Gore CJ, McSharry PE, Hewitt AJ, Saunders PU 2008, Scand J Med Sci Sports
design: Narrative review with re-analysis of ~100 years of match data
effect: In the first days at 3600 m some players have AMS symptoms and VO2max is ~25% reduced; home advantage above ~2000 m is 'more than compensated' by sea-level teams winning at home against the same opponents; 1-2 weeks at altitude is a reasonable preparation compromise.
limitations: Review; ~25% figure is a summary statement, not a soccer measurement.
relevance: Sets acute VO2max loss at 3600 m; supports 'no bonus for altitude teams at sea level'.

citation: Levine BD, Stray-Gundersen J, Mehta RD 2008, Scand J Med Sci Sports
design: Narrative review
effect: Two parallel pathways: (a) hypoxia lowers VO2max, raises relative intensity of any given work rate and delays recovery of high-energy phosphates between high-intensity efforts; (b) lower air density reduces drag (helps high-velocity running) but alters ball drag and lift, impairing sensorimotor skills. Effects largest early in exposure and reduced by acclimatisation.
limitations: Review; no new data.
relevance: Framework used by this project to separate physiology from ball flight.

citation: Girard O, Amann M, Aughey R, Billaut F, Bishop DJ, Bourdon P et al. 2013, Br J Sports Med (position statement)
design: Position statement
effect: Summarises current knowledge on altitude and team sports; recommends strategies to improve acclimatisation when competing at altitude; flags many unresolved issues.
limitations: Position statement; not quantitative.
relevance: Context; confirms evidence gaps for team sports.

citation: Wehrlin JP, Hallén J 2006, Eur J Appl Physiol
design: Within-subject incremental tests at each altitude
effect: VO2max declined linearly from 66 ± 1.6 mL/kg/min at 300 m to 55 ± 1.6 at 2800 m = 6.3% per 1000 m (individual range 4.6-7.5% per 1000 m); already lower at 800 m than at 300 m; HRmax fell ~1.9 beats/min per 1000 m.
limitations: Endurance athletes, not soccer players; acute chamber exposure; n=8.
relevance: Primary slope used for the VO2max line in the model.

citation: Schuler B, Thomsen JJ, Gassmann M, Lundby C 2007, Scand J Med Sci Sports
exposure: Tested at sea level and on days 1, 7, 14, 21 at altitude
design: Longitudinal within-subject
effect: Day 1: VO2max -12.8%, time to exhaustion at 80% sea-level max power -25.8% (both p<0.05). Improvement ~4%/week (VO2max) and ~6%/week (time to exhaustion) over the first 14 days; no significant further gain from day 14 to 21 (+0.7% VO2max). Hb concentration and arterial O2 content rose with acclimatisation.
limitations: Cyclists, n=8; weekly improvement rates taken from a secondary summary of the paper.
relevance: Roughly half of the acute aerobic deficit recovers within two weeks; residual deficit persists.

citation: Saltin B, Larsen H, Terrados N, Bangsbo J et al. 1995, Scand J Med Sci Sports
population: Kenyan distance runners living/training at ~2000 m; Scandinavian runners
design: Cross-sectional physiological testing
effect: Altitude-resident Kenyan runners: VO2max 68 ± 1.4 mL/kg/min at ~2000 m vs 79.9 ± 1.4 at sea level (~15% lower at their home altitude).
limitations: Runners, not soccer; small groups.
relevance: Altitude residents are NOT unaffected: their aerobic ceiling is lower at altitude than it would be at sea level.

citation: Brutsaert TD 2008, Appl Physiol Nutr Metab
population: Review of high-altitude native populations (Andean, Tibetan)
design: Narrative review
effect: Indigenous high-altitude natives show higher mean VO2max in hypoxia and a smaller VO2max decrement with increasing hypoxia; insufficient evidence for better work economy or endurance capacity; higher exercise SaO2.
limitations: Review; developmental vs genetic origins unresolved.
relevance: Supports a partial (not complete) resident advantage.

citation: Balsom PD, Gaitanos GC, Ekblom B, Sjödin B 1994, Acta Physiol Scand
design: Within-subject 10 x 6 s cycle sprints, 30 s recovery
effect: Greater loss of pedalling speed across sprints in hypoxia (p<0.05); post-exercise lactate 10.3 vs 8.5 mmol/L; O2 uptake during sprints 6-9 lower (3.03 vs 3.19 L/min).
limitations: Non-athletes; cycling; n=7.
relevance: Repeated-sprint recovery is impaired under acute hypoxia; first sprints unaffected.

citation: Goods PSR, Dawson BT, Landers GJ, Gore CJ, Peeling P 2014, Int J Sports Physiol Perform
design: Randomised within-subject; 3 sets of 9 x 4 s treadmill sprints
effect: Total work highest at sea level and lower at each successive altitude (SL > 2000 > 3000 > 4000 m, p<0.05). First-set mean power reduced only at 4000 m; in later sets mean power reduced at ALL altitudes. Peak power maintained except set 3 at 4000 m.
limitations: Simulated altitude; magnitudes not in abstract; n=10.
relevance: Direct team-sport evidence: single/early sprints preserved, repeated-effort recovery degraded even at 2000 m.

citation: Townsend N, Brocherie F, Millet GP, Girard O 2020, Exp Physiol
altitude: FiO2 0.21 / 0.17 (~1900 m equiv.) / 0.13 (~3600 m equiv.), normobaric
design: Within-subject 8 x 5 s treadmill sprints (25 s recovery) + neuromuscular testing
effect: Mean sprint distance 22.9 m (SL) vs 22.7 m (moderate, n.s.) vs 22.3 m (severe, p=0.04; ~-2.6%). Peripheral (muscle) fatigue indices higher in severe hypoxia; no additional central fatigue.
limitations: Not soccer players; simulated altitude; short protocol.
relevance: Small repeated-sprint cost at ~3600 m-equivalent, negligible at ~1900 m-equivalent for a short set.

citation: Billaut F, Smith K 2010, Int J Sports Physiol Perform
design: 20 x 5 s cycle sprints, 25 s rest; pulse oximetry, EMG
effect: Mechanical work fell 23.5% over sprints; arterial O2 saturation fell 3.5%; changes in SaO2 tracked work loss (R^2 = 0.68).
limitations: Sea-level study; mechanism only.
relevance: Shows that O2 availability regulates repeated-sprint fatigue in soccer players — the pathway altitude acts on.

citation: Linthorne NP 2016, Sports
design: De-trended, wind-corrected competition analysis
effect: 100 m time advantage at 2250 m: 0.19 ± 0.02 s men, 0.21 ± 0.05 s women (~1.9-2.0%); ~0.10 s per 1000 m, equivalent to a 2 m/s tail wind.
limitations: Athletics 100 m (10 s of near-max speed); soccer sprints are 10-30 m where drag saving is smaller.
relevance: Single maximal sprint is slightly FASTER at altitude due to lower air density.

citation: Hollings SC, Hopkins WG, Hume PA 2012, Eur J Sport Sci
altitude: Venues from sea level to >1000 m
design: Mixed linear modelling of competition results
effect: Distance events 2-4% slower above 1000 m, with marginal impairment detectable even at ~150 m; mixed-model estimate of the 100 m advantage at Mexico City altitude ~0.10 s (about half of Linthorne's 0.19 s).
limitations: Athletics; values summarised from secondary sources citing the paper.
relevance: Direction and rough size of the sprint/endurance split with altitude.

citation: McMorris T, Hale BJ, Barwood M, Costello J, Corbett J 2017, Neurosci Biobehav Rev
population: 22 experiments in healthy humans (lab), exposure <=6 days
design: Systematic review and meta-regression
effect: Acute hypoxia impaired cognition with moderate effect (Hedges g = -0.49, 95% CI -0.64 to -0.34); low PaO2 (35-60 mmHg) was the key predictor (R^2 ~0.45); no difference between executive and non-executive tasks.
limitations: Lab cognition tasks at rest, not sport decision-making; low-PaO2 studies mostly correspond to altitudes well above 3000 m; corrigendum 2019 reclassified some studies.
relevance: Plausible small decision-making cost at high altitude; not quantifiable for soccer at 1500-2500 m -> 'insufficient evidence'.

citation: Goff JE 2013, Sports Engineering
population: Review of sport projectile aerodynamics (incl. soccer balls)
altitude: Physics: drag and Magnus force scale with air density
design: Narrative review
effect: Aerodynamic drag and lift/Magnus force are proportional to air density; lower density at altitude means less drag (ball travels further, faster) and less curve for the same spin.
limitations: Review; exact ball behaviour depends on ball model and speed regime (drag crisis).
relevance: Ball flight changes are physical and immediate; they affect both teams but favour the team more familiar with them.

citation: Chapman RF, Stray-Gundersen J, Levine BD 1998, J Appl Physiol
design: Retrospective responder / non-responder analysis + prospective confirmation
effect: Responders showed larger acute EPO rise, increased red-cell volume and VO2max; non-responders did not, and slowed interval-training velocity at altitude.
limitations: Runners; training camp context.
relevance: Individual responses to altitude differ substantially; team means hide large spread.

citation: Billaut F, Aughey RJ 2013, Br J Sports Med (update review)
design: Narrative review
effect: Summarises: 3.1% lower total distance at 1200-1753 m in the 2010 World Cup with top speed unchanged; 9% lower total distance and 15% lower high-velocity running 4 days after arrival at 1600 m in youth internationals; 1-2 weeks suggested for moderate altitude.
limitations: Review; relies on the primary studies above.
relevance: Source of the percentage values used for the 1600 m anchor; confirms single-effort speed is preserved.

citation: Alanis A, Salas O, Salas K, Quintero I, Carranza Y, Salazar L 2022, Apunts Sports Medicine
population: One Liga MX professional club (club not named), 130 league matches, Apertura 2014-Clausura 2018; outfield players completing 90 min
altitude: Liga MX venues grouped by FIFA zones: near sea level 0-500 m, low 501-2000 m, moderate 2001-3000 m (Toluca 2670 m, Mexico City ~2240 m, Pachuca, Puebla)
exposure: Normal league travel (typically arrival the day before; not controlled)
design: Retrospective camera-tracking (Match Analysis K2) comparison of team physical output and goals across altitude zones
effect: Per-player total distance essentially unchanged across zones: 9855 ± 836 m near sea level, 10102 ± 1930 m low altitude, 9878 ± 836 m moderate altitude; mean speed 6.26 / 6.40 / 6.22 km/h; sprints per player 19.2 / 20.5 / 19.4; time between sprints 5.30 / 5.06 / 5.38 min. No meaningful altitude penalty detected for this team.
limitations: Single club; players substituted or sent off excluded (survivorship); the club plays at moderate altitude every few weeks (habituation); Liga MX squads are largely Mexican and many players have altitude residency histories; numbers from abstract/results snippet, full text not read.
relevance: COUNTER-ANCHOR: a Liga MX team routinely exposed to 2000-3000 m showed no running deficit there. Supports the residency/habituation term in the model and warns against applying the sea-level-native penalty to Mexico-based clubs visiting Toluca.

citation: FIFA Executive Committee decisions on football at altitude, May 2007 - May 2008 (FIFA.com media release, 14 Mar 2008; contemporaneous news reports)
exposure: Acclimatisation rules: >2500 m three days strongly recommended; >2750 m one week mandatory; >3000 m generally not permitted unless two weeks' acclimatisation
design: Policy decision and revisions
effect: 27 May 2007: international matches banned above 2500 m (citing player health and unfair home advantage; affected La Paz 3600 m, Quito ~2800 m, Bogota ~2650 m, Cusco, and venues in Peru, Chile and Mexico incl. Toluca 2670 m). 27 Jun 2007: limit raised to 3000 m (Bogota, Quito allowed; La Paz, Cusco excluded); Jul 2007 provisional La Paz exemption. 15 Dec 2007 (Tokyo): tiered rule above (2500/2750/3000 m). 14 Mar 2008: tiered rule upheld. 27-29 May 2008: ban suspended after unanimous CONMEBOL protest (Brazil dissenting); Jun 2010 FIFA said altitude was no longer on its agenda.
limitations: Policy, not evidence; thresholds reflect the 2008 FIFA consensus (E14) and political negotiation rather than a measured performance cut-off; the 2670 m Toluca venue sat just above the original 2500 m limit and just below the later 2750 m tier.
relevance: Shows how the same physiology was translated into rules: the three FIFA tiers map directly onto the 'days since arrival' control (3 d / 7 d / 14 d).
